body.en:
Two geometric figures are similar (denoted by the symbol \( \sim \)) if they have the exact same shape, even if their sizes differ. Specifically, two polygons are similar if and only if:

  1. All corresponding angles are congruent (equal in measure).
  2. All corresponding side lengths are proportional, related by a constant ratio \( k \) known as the scale factor.

If \( \triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF \), the vertices are named in corresponding order: vertex \( A \) corresponds to \( D \), \( B \) to \( E \), and \( C \) to \( F \). The linear scale factor from \( \triangle ABC \) to \( \triangle DEF \) is:

\[ k = \frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{EF}{BC} = \frac{DF}{AC} \]

Every linear dimension (sides, altitudes, medians, perimeters) scales by \( k \). Areas scale by \( k^2 \), and volumes of similar 3D solids scale by \( k^3 \).

caption.en: When linear side lengths scale by k = 0.6, corresponding angles remain congruent (∠A ≅ ∠D, ∠B ≅ ∠E, ∠C ≅ ∠F), perimeters scale by k = 0.6, and areas scale by k² = 0.36.

label.en: ● Theorem 4.1 — Triangle Similarity Criteria (AA, SAS, SSS)

body.en:
While general polygons require checking both all angles and all side ratios, triangles need only one of three minimal criteria:

  • AA (Angle-Angle): If two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another, the third angles are automatically congruent (since angles sum to \(180^\circ\)), and the triangles are similar.
  • SAS (Side-Angle-Side): If two pairs of corresponding sides are proportional and their included angle is congruent: \( \frac{A'B'}{AB} = \frac{A'C'}{AC} \) and \( \angle A \cong \angle A' \).
  • SSS (Side-Side-Side): If all three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same constant ratio: \( \frac{A'B'}{AB} = \frac{B'C'}{BC} = \frac{C'A'}{CA} = k \).

label.en: Common Pitfall — The SSA Non-Similarity Trap

body.en: Two proportional sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do NOT prove triangle similarity. Just as in congruence, the non-included angle allows the third side to swing into two distinct orientations (acute or obtuse), producing non-similar triangles. Similarity requires the congruent angle to be strictly sandwiched between the proportional sides (SAS).

If a line is parallel to one side of a triangle intersecting the other two sides, it divides the two sides proportionally:

\[ \text{In } \triangle ABC, \text{ if } DE \parallel BC \implies \frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC} \quad (\text{Part-to-Part Proportionality}) \]

Furthermore, because \( \angle ADE \cong \angle B \) and \( \angle AED \cong \angle C \) (corresponding angles formed by parallel lines), \( \triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC \) by AA similarity. Therefore, the transversal base satisfies the Whole-to-Part ratio:

\[ \frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{DE}{BC} \]

caption.en: Segment DE is parallel to base BC (marked with >> chevrons). Part-to-part ratio: AD/DB = 12/8 = 1.5, matching AE/EC = 15/10 = 1.5. Whole-to-part ratio: AD/AB = 12/20 = 0.6, which equals DE/BC = 18/30 = 0.6.

label.en: Worked Example 4.1 — Parallel Transversal with Unknown Length

body.en:
In \( \triangle ABC \), segment \( DE \parallel BC \) with \( D \) on \( AB \) and \( E \) on \( AC \). If \( AD = 8 \), \( DB = 12 \), and \( DE = 6 \), find the length of base \( BC \).

Step 1: Identify the correct ratio. The parallel segments \( DE \) and \( BC \) are sides of \( \triangle ADE \) and \( \triangle ABC \). Side ratios must use whole sides from vertex \( A \), not part-to-part segments:

\[ AB = AD + DB = 8 + 12 = 20 \]

Step 2: Set up the whole-to-part proportion:

\[ \frac{DE}{BC} = \frac{AD}{AB} \implies \frac{6}{BC} = \frac{8}{20} \]

Step 3: Solve for \( BC \):

\[ BC = \frac{6 \times 20}{8} = \frac{120}{8} = 15 \]

When segments \( AC \) and \( BD \) intersect at point \( E \) and their bases are parallel (\( AB \parallel CD \)), the resulting figure forms an hourglass / bowtie shape. Because:

  1. \( \angle AEB \cong \angle CED \) (vertical angles are equal), and
  2. \( \angle A \cong \angle C \) and \( \angle B \cong \angle D \) (alternate interior angles formed by parallel lines),

the two triangles are similar by AA similarity: \( \triangle ABE \sim \triangle CDE \). Corresponding sides yield:

\[ \frac{AB}{CD} = \frac{AE}{CE} = \frac{BE}{DE} \]

caption.en: Parallel bases AB and CD (marked with >> chevrons) guarantee △ABE ~ △CDE. Vertical angles at E are congruent. Cross-proportions: AE/EC = BE/ED = AB/CD = 0.65.

label.en: ● Theorem 4.4 — Right Triangle Altitude Theorem (Geometric Mean)

body.en:
In a right triangle \( \triangle ABC \) with right angle at \( C \), the altitude \( CD = h \) drawn perpendicular to the hypotenuse \( AB = c \) divides the hypotenuse into two segments \( p = AD \) and \( q = DB \). This altitude splits the original triangle into two smaller right triangles that are both similar to the original and to each other: \( \triangle ACD \sim \triangle CBD \sim \triangle ABC \).

This yields three fundamental geometric mean relationships:

  1. Altitude Rule: The altitude is the geometric mean of the two hypotenuse segments:
    \[ h^2 = p \cdot q \iff h = \sqrt{p \cdot q} \]
  2. Leg Rules: Each leg is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and the adjacent segment:
    \[ b^2 = c \cdot p \quad \text{and} \quad a^2 = c \cdot q \]
  3. Area / Product Rule: Comparing area computed using legs versus hypotenuse and altitude:
    \[ \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}ab = \frac{1}{2}ch \implies a \cdot b = c \cdot h \]

title.en: Altitude to the Hypotenuse & Geometric Mean

caption.en: In right △ABC (hypotenuse c = 25), altitude CD = 12 divides AB into p = 9 and q = 16. Altitude rule: h² = 9 × 16 = 144 = 12². Leg rules: b² = 25 × 9 = 225 = 15² and a² = 25 × 16 = 400 = 20².

body.en:
In any triangle \( \triangle ABC \), the ray bisecting an interior angle divides the opposite side into two segments proportional to the other two adjacent sides:

\[ \text{If ray } AD \text{ bisects } \angle A \text{ with } D \text{ on } BC \implies \frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{AB}{AC} \]

caption.en: Ray AD bisects ∠BAC (marked with ticked angle arcs). The base segments BD and DC are in the exact same proportion as the adjacent sides: BD/DC = 6/9 = 2/3, matching AB/AC = 12/18 = 2/3.

label.en: Exam Trap — Overlapping Inverted Triangles (Shared Angle)

body.en:
A notorious standardized exam trap involves an interior transversal \( DE \) that is NOT parallel to base \( BC \), but is drawn such that \( \angle ADE \cong \angle C \). Because \( \angle A \) is shared, \( \triangle ADE \sim \triangle ACB \) by AA similarity — but in inverted orientation!

\[ \frac{AD}{AC} = \frac{AE}{AB} = \frac{DE}{BC} \]

Students who reflexively assume \( DE \parallel BC \) and write \( \frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC} \) will get the question wrong. Always check angle markings carefully before setting up proportions.

caption.en: Notice that DE is NOT parallel to BC. Angle ADE ≅ ∠C (double arc) and ∠A is shared. Therefore △ADE ~ △ACB in inverted order: AD/AC = 6/12 = 0.5, AE/AB = 8/16 = 0.5, and DE/BC = 7/14 = 0.5.

label.en: Worked Example 4.2 — Realistic Indirect Measurement via Shadows

body.en:
A 6-foot surveyor stands on level ground and casts an 8-foot shadow. At the exact same moment, a nearby radio communications tower casts a 60-foot shadow. How tall is the radio tower?

Step 1: Verify similarity. Sunlight rays strike level ground at the exact same angle \( \theta \) across the immediate vicinity. Both the surveyor and the tower stand perpendicular to the ground (\( 90^\circ \)). By AA similarity, the right triangles formed by the object height and shadow length are similar.

Step 2: Set up the proportion:

\[ \frac{\text{Height of Tower}}{\text{Shadow of Tower}} = \frac{\text{Height of Surveyor}}{\text{Shadow of Surveyor}} \implies \frac{H}{60} = \frac{6}{8} \]

Step 3: Solve for \( H \):

\[ H = 60 \times \frac{3}{4} = 45\text{ feet}. \]

title.en: Indirect Measurement with Parallel Sunlight Rays

caption.en: Because sunlight rays arrive in parallel (dashed amber lines), both right triangles have the identical elevation angle θ = arctan(6/8) ≈ 36.9°. Proportions: H/60 = 6/8 ⇒ H = 45 ft.

body.en:
When two chords \( AB \) and \( CD \) intersect inside a circle at point \( P \), triangles \( \triangle PAC \) and \( \triangle PDB \) are similar by AA similarity:

  1. \( \angle APC \cong \angle DPB \) (vertical angles).
  2. \( \angle CAP \cong \angle BDP \) (inscribed angles intercepting the same arc \( BC \)).

Corresponding sides yield \( \frac{PA}{PD} = \frac{PC}{PB} \), establishing the Intersecting Chords Theorem:

\[ PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD \]

caption.en: Inscribed angles intercepting the same arc prove △PAC ~ △PDB. The product of chord segments is constant: PA × PB = 4 × 9 = 36, matching PC × PD = 6 × 6 = 36.

label.en: Worked Example C — Euclidean Distance & Orthogonal Projection

body.en:
A displacement has horizontal component \( \Delta x = 4 \) and vertical component \( \Delta y = 9 \). Find the squared magnitude \( d^2 \) and the area of the right triangle formed with the axes.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. By the Pythagorean theorem, \( d^2 = (4)^2 + (9)^2 = 16 + 81 = \mathbf{97} \).
  2. The enclosed right-triangle area is \( A = \frac{1}{2}(4)(9) = \mathbf{18} \).

label.en: Worked Example D — Euclidean Distance & Orthogonal Projection

body.en:
A displacement has horizontal component \( \Delta x = 5 \) and vertical component \( \Delta y = 5 \). Find the squared magnitude \( d^2 \) and the area of the right triangle formed with the axes.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. By the Pythagorean theorem, \( d^2 = (5)^2 + (5)^2 = 25 + 25 = \mathbf{50} \).
  2. The enclosed right-triangle area is \( A = \frac{1}{2}(5)(5) = \mathbf{12.5} \).

question.en: In right \( \triangle ABC \) with right angle at \( C \), altitude \( CD \) is drawn to hypotenuse \( AB \). If \( AD = 4 \) and \( DB = 9 \), find the length of leg \( BC \).

solution.en:
Step 1: Compute total hypotenuse \( AB \):

\[ AB = AD + DB = 4 + 9 = 13 \]

Step 2: Apply the Geometric Mean Leg Rule: The leg \( BC \) is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse \( AB \) and the adjacent segment \( DB \):

\[ BC^2 = AB \cdot DB = 13 \cdot 9 = 117 \]

Step 3: Simplify the radical:

\[ BC = \sqrt{117} = \sqrt{9 \times 13} = 3\sqrt{13} \approx 10.82 \]

question.en: Two similar cylinders have surface areas of \( 64\pi\ \text{cm}^2 \) and \( 144\pi\ \text{cm}^2 \). If the volume of the smaller cylinder is \( 96\pi\ \text{cm}^3 \), find the volume of the larger cylinder.

solution.en:
Step 1: Find the area ratio and linear scale factor \( k \):

\[ \frac{\text{Area}_2}{\text{Area}_1} = \frac{144\pi}{64\pi} = \frac{9}{4} = k^2 \implies k = \sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} = \frac{3}{2} \]

Step 2: Compute the volume ratio \( k^3 \):

\[ \frac{\text{Volume}_2}{\text{Volume}_1} = k^3 = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{27}{8} \]

Step 3: Calculate the volume of the larger cylinder:

\[ \text{Volume}_2 = 96\pi \times \frac{27}{8} = 12\pi \times 27 = 324\pi\ \text{cm}^3 \]

question.en: In \( \triangle PQR \), ray \( QS \) bisects \( \angle Q \) with \( S \) lying on side \( PR \). If \( PQ = 14 \), \( QR = 21 \), and \( PR = 25 \), find the length of segment \( PS \).

solution.en:
Step 1: Apply the Angle Bisector Theorem: The bisector divides side \( PR \) into segments proportional to the adjacent sides:

\[ \frac{PS}{SR} = \frac{PQ}{QR} = \frac{14}{21} = \frac{2}{3} \]

Step 2: Express \( SR \) in terms of \( PS \): Since \( PS + SR = 25 \), we have \( SR = 25 - PS \):

\[ \frac{PS}{25 - PS} = \frac{2}{3} \implies 3PS = 2(25 - PS) = 50 - 2PS \]

Step 3: Solve for \( PS \):

\[ 5PS = 50 \implies PS = 10 \quad (\text{and } SR = 15). \]

question.en: [Similarity & Proportional Reasoning · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
